name: Gliclazide
reviewed_by: William Gregory M. Rivero, MD, FPCP, DPSN
drafted_by: AI-assisted draft (Claude) for review by Dr. W. Rivero

usual_adult_dose.dose: 30 mg once daily at breakfast to start; increase stepwise (60, 90, 120 mg) at intervals of about 1 month (or after 2 weeks if glucose has not fallen); maximum 120 mg/day

Start 40–80 mg/day before breakfast; usual maintenance 80–160 mg/day in 2 doses (before breakfast and dinner); maximum 320 mg/day; caution above 160 mg/day, particularly with kidney impairment (IR SmPC)
One 80 mg immediate-release tablet is comparable to 30 mg MR; monitor glucose when switching

key_interactions.effect: Strong rise in hypoglycemia risk, possibly coma.
Phenylbutazone and alcohol increase hypoglycemia; danazol raises glucose.
key_interactions.action: Not recommended; choose alternatives or monitor glucose and adjust the dose.

key_interactions.effect: Dysglycemia (hypo- or hyperglycemia), especially in older adults.

key_interactions.drug_or_class: Insulin, metformin, beta-blockers, fluconazole, NSAIDs, clarithromycin, MAO inhibitors
key_interactions.action: Monitor glucose; lower the gliclazide dose if needed.

key_interactions.effect: Sulfonylureas may increase the anticoagulant effect.
key_interactions.action: Monitor the international normalized ratio (INR); adjust the anticoagulant.

key_interactions.drug_or_class: Glucocorticoids, high-dose chlorpromazine, St John's wort
key_interactions.effect: Raise glucose or lower gliclazide exposure.

common: Hypoglycemia (especially with irregular or skipped meals)
Gastrointestinal upset: abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, diarrhea, constipation (uncommon)
serious: Severe or prolonged hypoglycemia needing hospital care
Blood disorders (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, granulocytopenia; agranulocytosis and hemolytic anemia as class effects)
Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to gliclazide, other sulfonylureas or sulfonamides
Type 1 diabetes; diabetic precoma or coma; diabetic ketoacidosis
Severe renal or hepatic insufficiency (use insulin)
monitoring: Hypoglycemia symptoms, especially in older adults, poor intake and kidney impairment
G6PD deficiency: sulfonylureas can cause hemolytic anemia; use with caution and consider a non-sulfonylurea alternative (SmPC 4.4)

pk.bioavailability: Completely absorbed; food does not affect absorption (MR SmPC)
pk.peak: MR: plasma levels rise over 6 hours and plateau from 6 to 12 hours
pk.half_life: MR: 12 to 20 hours; immediate-release: mean 10 hours
pk.half_life_eskd: Immediate-release SmPC: prolonged slightly, not significantly, in renal insufficiency; not quantified
pk.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism (enzymes not named in SmPC)
pk.excretion_renal_pct: Metabolites mainly in urine; under 1% unchanged

revision_log.change: IR maintenance given in 2 doses; caution above 160 mg/day.
